opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think of them as really two views of the same object. An environment is basically a task, or a distribution of tasks, plus some harness for the model to interact with, whether that's tools, a sandbox, or a multi-turn conversation, plus some way of scoring what happened. If you have those pieces, you have an eval. And if you have an eval, you're most of the way to having an RL environment, because RL just needs that same loop: the model acts, the environment responds, and at the end you get a reward signal.

The difference is mostly in what you care about. For evaluation, you want the score to be a faithful measurement. You want it to be hard to game, reasonably stable, and to reflect the capability you actually care about. For RL, you care about those things too, maybe even more, because the model will find every crack in your reward function. But you also care about things like whether the task sits at the right difficulty for the model to learn from. If the model gets zero percent or a hundred percent, there's no signal. You want tasks in that middle zone where some rollouts succeed and some don't, so there's something to push on.

So in practice, a lot of good RL environments start life as evals. Someone builds a benchmark to measure, say, how well a model can navigate a codebase or use a set of tools, and then people realize they can train against a version of it. That's part of why I think it's valuable to build these things in a modular, shareable way, where the same environment definition can be used for both. You write the task, the harness, and the rubric once, and then you can either run it to get a number or plug it into a trainer.

The caveat is the usual Goodhart problem. Once you train on an environment, it's no longer a clean eval for that model. So you want held-out splits, or separate environments that test the same underlying skill in a different form. But conceptually, I don't think there's a hard line between them. Evals are environments you measure with, and RL environments are evals you learn from.

r001.rationale: The response says RL environments often start as evals and that the same environment definition can be run for evaluation or plugged into a trainer.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that they're the same thing, and the fact that we've historically treated them as separate is mostly an accident of how the field developed. An eval is an environment where you only ever run one episode and never update the model. An RL environment is an eval where you actually let the gradient flow back. The core pieces are identical: you have some task, you have a way to present it to the model, the model takes actions, and at the end there's a function that tells you how well it did. Whether you call that function a "score" or a "reward" is really just a question of what you do with the number afterward.

Where it gets more interesting is when you start thinking about what makes a good one of each, because the requirements actually pull in slightly different directions. For an eval, you want it to be stable and hard to game, you want it to be a fixed target so you can compare across models and across time. For an RL environment, you want it to be hard to game too, but you also want it to have a learning signal at the model's current level. If the reward is zero on every rollout, you're not going to learn anything. So a lot of what makes a great RL environment is about having a curriculum built in, or having partial credit, or having a distribution of difficulty where the model can get a foothold and then climb.

And the other big difference is that in RL, the environment is going to get hammered by an optimizer. Whatever cracks are in your reward function, the model will find them, because that's literally what the training process is doing. With an eval you can get away with a slightly sloppy grader because the model wasn't trained against it. With RL you can't. So I think of RL environments as evals that have been stress-tested by an adversary.

What I'd actually like to see is people building these things with both uses in mind from the start. You write the environment once, you hold out some of it as an eval, you train on the rest, and the fact that the eval is in the same format as the training environment means you get a really clean read on generalization. The split between "benchmarks" and "training data" has made us lazy about that. The thing we should be building is just environments, and then deciding per environment whether we're measuring or training.

r001.rationale: The response says to build the environment once, hold out part for evaluation, and train on the rest, making the same environment usable for both evaluation and RL training.

astra-6.text:
I think they’re very closely related. In both cases, you need some setting where the model can take actions and you can measure how well it did. An evaluation environment lets you ask, “Can the model do this?” An RL environment lets you use that feedback to make the model better at it.

But there’s a gap between something that’s useful for evaluation and something that’s useful for training. For training, you need to run it repeatedly, generate enough variety, and have a reward signal that actually captures what you care about. If there’s a loophole in your evaluator, training puts a lot of pressure on finding it.

So I tend to think of them as the same underlying kind of infrastructure, serving different purposes. You want environments you can learn from, but you also need held-out tasks and environments that tell you whether that learning generalizes.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes evaluation and RL environments as related infrastructure with different purposes, and calls for held-out tasks. It does not state that the same offline evaluation test set can also be used as the RL training set.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they’re very closely related. An evaluation environment gives the model something to do and some way of measuring how well it did. A reinforcement learning environment needs those same things, but you use that feedback to update the model. So, in principle, a lot of environments that are useful for evaluation can also be useful for training.

The distinction is what you want to learn from the result. In training, you want an environment that produces a useful learning signal. In evaluation, you want to know whether the model can handle something it hasn’t already been optimized to handle. Once you train on an evaluation, improvement on that evaluation becomes harder to interpret. You still need held-out tasks or environments to tell whether the model learned a general capability or just got better at that particular setup.

r001.rationale: The response says evaluation environments can also be used for training and specifically notes that training on an evaluation changes how its results should be interpreted.
